titel: The rule of 72 and other mental arithmetic aids
kurz: How interest rates can be converted into doubling times without a calculator, and how large the error of these rules of thumb is.

bloecke.md:
A percentage on its own says little. 4% is half as much as 8%, and over one year that is also true. Over thirty years, an amount grows 3.2-fold at 4% and 10.1-fold at 8%, a ratio of about one to three. Comparing such offers therefore requires a conversion that works in your head. Most decisions are made in conversation, at an advisory appointment or while reading an advertisement, and only rarely at a desk with a spreadsheet.

The most suitable measure is the number of years it takes for an amount to double. This number allows interest on savings, loan interest, the inflation rate and a fund prospectus to be compared directly, and it can be found with a single division.

bloecke.formel: t = ln(2) / ln(1 + i)    ≈    72 / i (as a percentage)
bloecke.erklaerung: ln(2) is 0.693. For small interest rates, ln(1+i) is approximately equal to i, which gives t ≈ 69.3 / i. Because ln(1+i) is always slightly smaller than i, the exact doubling time is longer than this first approximation. The numerator is therefore adjusted upwards.
variablen: interest rate or return per year, constant
bloecke.beispiel: At 6%, the rule gives 72 / 6 = 12 years; the exact figure is 11.90 years.

bloecke.md: There are two reasons for using 72 instead of 69.3 in the numerator. First, 72 is divisible by 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 9 and 12, that is, by the interest rates that come up in everyday life. Second, the larger numerator compensates for the curvature of the logarithm. The approximation is exact at 7.85%, right in the middle of the historical range of equity returns. At lower rates, the rule estimates the doubling time slightly too long, and at higher rates too short. The 72 is thus deliberately tuned to this range.

bloecke.titel: Deviation of the rule of 72 from the exact value
bloecke.unter: Positive values mean that the rule estimates the doubling time too long; between 4% and 12%, the error stays below 2%.

serien.name: Deviation from the exact doubling time in %

bloecke.md:
At high rates from about 15% upwards, the estimate turns out too optimistic. The rule then gives a shorter doubling time than the exact calculation: 3.6 instead of 3.8 years at 20%.

The rule does not apply to savings plans, because it refers to an amount invested once. With monthly contributions, the capital doubles much faster at first, but because of the contributions and not because of the interest.

In addition, the denominator must be the interest rate per period. 72 divided by a monthly rate of 1% gives 72 months, not 72 years.

## Other target multiples

The same derivation works for any target multiple. Instead of ln(2), the numerator is then ln(3), ln(4) or ln(10), and instead of 72 you get a different rule-of-thumb number. The best known is 114 for tripling. Quadrupling corresponds to two doublings, so its rule-of-thumb number is 144.

bloecke.titel: Rule-of-thumb numbers for other target multiples

bloecke.md: Years times return divided by 72 gives the **number of doublings**. The capital multiple, that is, the multiple of the initial capital, is then 2 to the power of this number. Useful reference values are 2 to the power of 0.5 equals 1.41 and 2 to the power of 0.25 equals 1.19, and for whole doublings 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 and 64.

25 × 6 / 72 = 2.08 doublings. That is two full doublings (factor 4) and a small remainder, a factor of around 4.24 in total. €10,000 thus becomes about €42,400.

The exact calculation, 10,000 × 1.06 to the power of 25, gives €42,919. The estimation error is 1.2%, far below the uncertainty of the return assumption itself.

bloecke.titel: Final value of one euro by interest rate and term
bloecke.unter: The cells show the exact capital multiples (1+i) to the power of n; counting doublings with the rule of 72 hits these values to within a few per cent across the whole grid.

bloecke.md:
## The rule of 70 for prices

For inflation rates, the range below 5% matters most, and there the 72 gives times that are too long. The **rule of 70**, with 70 in the numerator, is therefore commonly used. It indicates after how many years the price level doubles. That is also the time in which the [[Purchasing power|purchasing power]] of a balance that earns no interest halves.

In August 2026, the German inflation rate was 2.9% compared with the same month a year earlier. 70 / 2.9 gives 24 years; the exact figure is 24.2. Over the long term, from 1997 to 2025, the harmonised index of consumer prices rose by an average of 1.94% a year, which gives 36 years. In the exceptional year 2022, with 6.9%, it would have been ten years.

With inflation at a constant 2.9% and zero interest, €10,000 retains purchasing power of around €5,035 after 24 years.

Interest reduces this loss but does not offset it. The ECB deposit facility rate has stood at 2.50% since 16 September 2026. The nominal interest rate minus the inflation rate gives around −0.4%. Balances therefore grow in nominal terms, but their purchasing power still falls.

## A rule-of-thumb figure for equities

A value of around 5% has become established as a working assumption for the long-term real return on broadly diversified equities. The major data series support this order of magnitude. World equities returned 5.2% a year in real terms from 1900 to 2024 (Dimson/Marsh/Staunton), and US equities 6.6% in real terms from 1900 to 2025. For German investors, calculated using German inflation, the real return on the MSCI World from 1997 to 2025 was 6.0%, and that on the DAX 5.6%.

At 5% real, purchasing power doubles roughly every 14 years according to the rule of 72. This value is an average over decades and not a promise for the next period. In euros, the MSCI World returned minus 3.8% a year from 2000 to 2009 and plus 11.3% from 2016 to 2025. The rule of thumb therefore describes the long-term trend and says little about the course of individual decades.

bloecke.unter: The doubling times are calculated exactly from long-term real returns: for world equities and world bonds for 1900-2024, for US assets and gold for 1900-2025 (DMS/UBS), and for the DAX and MSCI World for 1997-2025 based on the German HICP.

bloecke.md:
## Percentages in your head

The doubling rule requires confident percentage arithmetic. Five methods cover almost all cases:

- The simplest route is via 1%. To do this, move the decimal point two places to the left and then multiply. 17% of €2,400 is 24 × 17 = €408.
- The percentage and the base value can be swapped, because x% of y is the same as y% of x. 8% of 25 is 25% of 8, which is 2. The second calculation is quicker.
- A [[Basis point|basis point]] is one hundredth of a percentage point. A fund fee of 7 basis points costs €7 a year on €10,000, and 150 basis points cost €150.
- Percentages and percentage points must be kept apart. If a ratio rises from 2% to 3%, that is an increase of one percentage point, but of 50%.
- Small rates can be added, large ones cannot. Two years of 2% each give 4.04%, so addition is good enough here. Two years of 30% each give 69% instead of 60%. From about 10% upwards, you therefore have to multiply.

The rule can also be reversed. If the overall multiple is known, divide the number of doublings by the number of years and multiply by 72. A portfolio that has tripled in ten years corresponds to 1.58 doublings. 72 × 1.58 / 10 gives around 11.4% a year. The naive calculation “200% divided by ten years equals 20%” gives a value almost twice as high. A related calculation uses the reciprocal. A price-to-earnings ratio of 20 corresponds to an earnings yield of 1/20, or 5%.

An advertised return of 6% is the gross figure before costs and before inflation. After 1.5% in fees, 4.4% remains, and after 2% inflation, 2.4% remains in real terms.

The doubling time thus lengthens from 12 to around 30 years. The rule only gives a useful result with a return adjusted for costs and inflation.

The deviation at high rates can be largely eliminated with a correction term from the series expansion of the logarithm: t ≈ 69.3 / i + 0.35 (at 20%, this approximation gives 3.815 years compared with exactly 3.802 years, and at 2% exactly 35.0 years). Up to just under 10%, the error stays below one per mille; at 20%, it is 3.5 per mille.

With continuous compounding, as is usual in financial models, no correction is needed. There, t = ln(2)/r, that is, exactly 69.3 divided by the rate as a percentage. The 72 is designed for the annual crediting of interest that is usual in practice.

1. Divide every return you are quoted by 72 straight away and remember the result as a doubling time.
2. Do the same calculation for every loan offer. At a mortgage rate of 3.97% (offer rate according to Dr. Klein on 3 September 2026, ten-year fixed-rate period), a debt on which nothing is repaid doubles in 18 years. The statutory default interest rate (Verzugszins) of 6.52% for consumers, by contrast, is calculated without compound interest (Section 289 BGB, Civil Code) and doubles a debt only after just over 15 years (100 / 6.52).
3. For periods of more than ten years, also deduct inflation before dividing. Only then does the result describe the doubling of purchasing power and not merely that of the euro amount.

mitnehmen: 72 divided by the interest rate as a percentage gives the doubling time in years, with an error of less than 2% between 4% and 12%.
For inflation and other low rates, 70 works better as the numerator; for tripling, the number is 114, and for a tenfold increase, 240.
Years times return divided by 72 gives the number of doublings, and 2 raised to the power of this number is the capital multiple.
In real terms, the purchasing power of broadly diversified equities has historically doubled roughly every 12 to 14 years; for a balance earning the current deposit facility rate, it does not double.
Costs and inflation are deducted before dividing, because the rule is only as accurate as the return you put in.

begriffe.text: The period in which capital doubles at a constant rate of interest. It is t = ln(2) / ln(1+i).
An approximation of the doubling time in which 72 is divided by the interest rate as a percentage. It is exact at 7.85% and usable between 1% and 15%.
A variant of the doubling rule with 70 in the numerator. It is more accurate at low rates and is therefore usually used for inflation and loss of purchasing power.
One hundredth of a percentage point. 25 basis points are 0.25 percentage points. Fees and interest rate steps are usually stated in basis points.
The quantity of goods that can be bought with a sum of money. With inflation, it falls even when the nominal amount grows.
